Building an AI-powered app at a young age taught me one big lesson. Technology is only useful if it respects the user. Too many apps are designed to keep you scrolling as long as possible. Most news apps measure success by how long you keep scrolling. It makes sense from a business perspective, but it often leads to algorithms that push outrage or endless doomscrolling just to keep your attention pinned to the screen.

At Headlinne, we made a different choice. Our engineering team built our feed to optimize for relevance and clarity instead of duration. We want you to find what you need to know quickly, understand the context, and then get on with your day.

This meant rebuilding how we rank stories. Instead of looking for what triggers the strongest emotional reaction, our system looks for signal-to-noise ratio. It prioritizes factual updates and diverse perspectives over engagement spikes. It is a slower way to build an app, but it is the only way to build a product that respects your time.

We believe the future of AI in news isn't about keeping you trapped in a feed. It is about being a useful tool that helps you stay informed without the clutter.

Automotive and robotics news also caught our attention. Tesla is facing its largest recall yet, affecting about 3 million vehicles. Most issues involve door handles and will be addressed through over-the-air updates, though some will require physical stickers and camera adjustments. Meanwhile, in China, a humanoid robot named Lightning completed a 100-meter sprint in 9.32 seconds, officially beating Usain Bolt’s long-standing world record.

On the regulatory front, TikTok has agreed to a $400 million settlement with the U.S. Department of Justice. The lawsuit alleged that the platform violated the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act by collecting data from minors without obtaining proper parental consent.

Finally, looking toward the stars, NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is getting ready to launch. It is expected to identify up to 200,000 new planets and provide new data on the mysteries of dark matter and dark energy.

So we changed the goal of our algorithm. Instead of maximizing your time on screen, we optimize for information density. We want you to understand the world better, not just consume more content. If you open our app, read two stories that actually matter to you, and then feel informed enough to put your phone down, we consider that a success.

This required a different engineering approach. We had to focus on relevance and summary quality rather than rage bait or clickbait. It is a harder path to build, but it is the only way to make a news product that respects your time instead of stealing it.

We believe technology should serve your curiosity, not manipulate your attention span.
